source.title: Explaining Memorization and Generalization: A Large-Scale Study with Coherent Gradients
source.authors: Piotr Zieliński; Shankar Krishnan; Satrajit Chatterjee

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: Tests label-noise and memorization predictions on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 using new gradient-suppression methods and large convolutional networks; the label-noise experiments also report standard SGD results.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own label-noise results. Cited findings from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are not rows. Figure 1 and Appendix A provide training curves; Section 2 explicitly says the 100% noise curve shows the network memorizes the whole training set. RM3 and winsorization are altered training methods, so their outcomes are recorded as method-specific results.
record.test_reason: The standard-SGD experiments directly repeat label randomization and measure training accuracy and learning dynamics. They bear on V1, the slowing component of V2, parts of V4, and V6. The gradient-suppression experiments primarily evaluate the authors' intervention.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors interpret their noise and natural-difficulty experiments as evidence for coherent gradients at scale. Standard SGD memorizes randomized labels, while suppressing weak gradient directions reduces memorization and disproportionately impairs corrupt or difficult examples. They conclude that common patterns are learned first.
record.recipe_differences: Uses ImageNet and CIFAR-10 with large convolutional networks and label-noise accuracy curves; adds RM3, M3, RA3 and CIFAR-10 winsorization experiments. The standard-SGD label-noise runs resemble the original intervention, but the study's primary new tests use different methods and datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and noise fraction; optimizer/gradient aggregation method; batch size; learning-rate schedule; momentum. The study notes RM3's batch size matters and that weak-gradient suppression can make training less stable.

fits_no_version.finding: RM3 reduces generalization gaps and inhibits corrupt-label fitting; winsorization prevents fitting fully randomized CIFAR-10 labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing weak gradient directions can reduce memorization under modified training algorithms.

fits_no_version.finding: RM3 fits naturally easy examples more accurately than naturally hard examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-gradient suppression disproportionately impairs learning of naturally difficult examples.

fits_no_version.finding: True-label pretraining reduces the time to reach 90% random-label accuracy from 81 to 62 epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Features learned from true labels can accelerate subsequent random-label memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: Easy examples generalize better among themselves; a model trained on hard examples achieves 44% on easy test examples versus 85% for easy-trained models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Naturally occurring example difficulty predicts generalization and does not follow a simple nested decision-boundary interpretation.

record.problems: Most ImageNet outcomes are shown in plots without exact values; authors report no error bars and state they did not perform hyperparameter search. Some additional random-label results use altered optimizers and should not be generalized to standard SGD.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified rows were extracted for 25%, 50%, and 75% SGD training/test accuracy because the figures supply curves without text values and the 5-level sweep is summarized in aggregate rows R2, R7, and R9. Appendix A shows corresponding train/test loss and pristine/corrupt curves; those additional plotted measures are not separately extracted. RM3 and RA3 comparisons at 0%, 50%, and 100% noise are not fully itemized beyond results relevant to the claim versions.

untested.parts: Exact chance-level test error is not recoverable from the supplied plot transcription. Within each ImageNet architecture, the recipe is held fixed across noise levels.
The small constant-factor training-time comparison between true and fully randomized labels is not quantified. The 62-versus-81-epoch comparison changes initialization while keeping random labels.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
The complete cross-noise test-error trajectory and exact chance endpoint cannot be established from the supplied figure transcription.

No controlled comparison establishes whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent random-label fitting, or how removing them changes true-label generalization. Their omission alone does not test these comparisons.

missing.what: A qualitative learning-rate result: increasing label noise slows learning, including learning of pristine examples. These are learning dynamics, not changes to the optimizer's scheduled learning-rate parameter.
missing.locator: Section 2 predictions and stated experimental confirmation; Figures 1, 6 and 7

missing.what: The explicit finding that pristine examples are learned faster than corrupt examples. Existing rows omit this ordering, and rows_left_out declares omitted plotted measures rather than recording this qualitative result.
missing.locator: Section 2 predictions and stated experimental confirmation; Figures 1(c–d), 6(c–d) and 7(c–d)

missing.what: A separate standard-SGD comparator at 50% noise: high training accuracy on both pristine and corrupt examples. R4 currently records only RM3's outcome.

record.verdict_notes: No scope-limiting verdict follows merely from unavailable plot values. RM3 and winsorization outcomes evaluate deliberate memorization-suppression methods and do not challenge the unchanged standard-SGD claims. The study is not an original source for these versions.

versions.untested_parts: Tests completely randomized labels on ImageNet and CIFAR-10, but does not report chance-level test error as an exact number or test every standard architecture and optimizer.
The text states that learning rates decrease as label noise increases, but does not give a true-label versus random-label training-time comparison suitable for extracting the claimed constant factor.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Tests 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% label noise on ImageNet; does not state exact train and test accuracies for each level in text. The reported noise sweep is not a statement that training accuracy remains perfect at every intermediate noise level.
Experiments without augmentation or weight decay are reported, but the study does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels. Dropout is not tested.
Does not test whether networks learn shared real-data patterns before memorizing noise over training; its easy/hard and label-noise experiments do not establish that ordering as stated.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD on ImageNet with randomized training labels; no augmentation or weight decay.
rows.value: The 100% noise curve shows the network memorizes the whole training set.
rows.note: Authors explicitly describe the 100% noise curve as full training-set memorization. The figure also plots test accuracy, but no exact chance-level value is stated.
rows.check: Full training-set memorization is explicitly stated. This establishes the fully randomized endpoint, not the entire V4 noise sweep or an exact chance-level test accuracy.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2, Figure 1 caption and paragraph on malignant overfitting; Appendix A training details.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD on ImageNet with randomized training labels; no augmentation or weight decay.
rows.measure: Training and test top-1 accuracy across noise levels
rows.note: The paper describes accuracy curves and states that test accuracy falls after reaching a maximum when label noise is present. It does not state exact values or say training accuracy is perfect at each intermediate noise level.
rows.check: The supplied figure transcription lacks readable curve values. Falling test accuracy over epochs is not the same as steadily rising test error across noise fractions; missing values do not establish partial fitting.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained with RM3 on ImageNet; rolling median of three mini-batch gradients.
rows.measure: Training and test top-1 accuracy; generalization gap
rows.baseline: SGD under the same noise level
rows.value: RM3 has a lower generalization gap than SGD.
rows.uncertainty: Experiments described as fairly consistent from run to run; error bars not shown.
rows.note: RM3 is an altered training method and does not itself establish standard SGD's behavior.
rows.check: A generalization-gap comparison for RM3 at zero noise evaluates the proposed method and does not measure the claimed noise-sweep behavior.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained with RM3 on ImageNet; rolling median of three mini-batch gradients.
rows.measure: Accuracy on pristine and corrupt training examples
rows.baseline: SGD under the same noise level
rows.value: RM3 achieves good accuracy only on pristine examples and does not learn corrupt examples.
rows.uncertainty: Experiments described as fairly consistent from run to run; error bars not shown.
rows.note: This is a negative result for RM3, not for standard SGD. SGD is described as achieving high training accuracy on both groups.
rows.check: This is a memorization-suppression intervention using a modified gradient estimator. Its failure to learn corrupt examples is not a counterexample to standard-SGD fitting. The accompanying SGD comparator should be extracted separately.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained with RM3 on ImageNet; rolling median of three mini-batch gradients.
rows.measure: Training and test top-1 accuracy; generalization gap
rows.baseline: SGD under the same noise level
rows.value: RM3 has a lower generalization gap than SGD.
rows.uncertainty: Experiments described as fairly consistent from run to run; error bars not shown.
rows.note: The text does not say RM3 fits the randomized training labels in this condition.
rows.check: A smaller generalization gap under RM3 does not establish either complete fitting or its absence. This is proposed-method performance.

rows.subject: Inception-V3
rows.operation_detail: Trained on ImageNet with randomized labels; no augmentation or weight decay. Section 2's preliminary experiment uses SGD.
rows.value: The results are essentially the same as those for ResNet-18; the 100% noise curve is shown.
rows.note: Appendix says label-noise results are essentially the same as ResNet-18; figure shows the training curve but gives no exact value in text.
rows.check: Appendix A reports essentially the same results as ResNet-18, supporting memorization at the fully randomized endpoint. Exact test accuracy is unavailable.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Trained with RM3; rolling median of three mini-batch gradients.
rows.baseline: SGD reaches correct classification on all examples after 90 epochs.
rows.value: Super hard examples: 61%; super easy examples: 99%.
rows.note: RM3 result shows incomplete fitting concentrated among harder examples; it is not a standard-SGD result.
rows.check: The condition is wrong: Section 4.3 uses original ImageNet labels, not 50% noise or a pristine/corrupt split. The reported accuracies are 61.01% for difficulty 8 and 99.15% for difficulty 0. This evaluates RM3 on naturally difficult examples.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with SGD and coordinate-wise winsorization of per-example gradients.
rows.baseline: s=0 is regular SGD with no clipping.
rows.value: The model completely memorizes the training data while generalizing very poorly.
rows.note: This provides an additional standard-SGD random-label result on CIFAR-10.
rows.check: Add V1. With s=0, this is ordinary SGD, and Appendix B explicitly reports complete memorization with poor generalization.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix B, paragraphs defining s=0 as regular SGD and describing complete memorization under 100% label noise; Figure 8.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with coordinate-wise winsorization of per-example gradients.
rows.baseline: s=0 regular SGD completely memorizes the training data.
rows.value: The model completely fails to learn the training set.
rows.note: Altered method; reported as strong validation for CGH.
rows.check: Failure to fit is explicitly reported, but under a gradient-clipping intervention designed to suppress memorization. It is not evidence against fitting with the unchanged standard training method.

rows.subject: ResNet-32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with coordinate-wise winsorization of per-example gradients.
rows.baseline: s=0 regular SGD completely memorizes the training data.
rows.value: SGD does not memorize the training set.
rows.note: The figure caption reports no memorization when clipping 2 or 4 extreme samples.
rows.check: The caption explicitly reports no memorization, but this is the proposed suppression intervention rather than standard-SGD behavior.
